title: How to go to a folder in Finder on Mac: shortcut, steps and fixes
metaTitle: How to Go to a Folder in Finder on Mac: Shortcut Guide
description: Learn how to go to a folder in Finder on Mac with Shift Command G, the Go menu, and typed paths. Steps, shortcuts and fixes for macOS 27.
targetKeyword: how to go to a folder in finder on mac
secondaryKeywords: how to open library folder mac
intro: To go to a folder in Finder on Mac, choose Go > Go to Folder or press ⇧⌘G, type the folder's path, and press Return. Finder then opens that folder, even when it sits several levels deep inside other folders.
tldr: Press ⇧⌘G in Finder, or choose Go > Go to Folder from the menu bar.
Type a path. Start with ~ for your home folder or / for the top level of the folder structure.
Matches appear as you type. Press Tab to accept one, then Return to open it.
A trailing slash, as in ~/Documents/, tells Finder the last part is a folder.
If the shortcut does nothing, click the desktop first so Finder is the active app.

blocks.text: Finder has a box for typing a location straight in. You skip the clicks through Documents, then a project folder, then a subfolder you need once a month. You type the path, press Return, and Finder opens the folder. Nothing needs installing. The box is part of macOS, and it works as long as Finder is the active app.
The fastest route: Go to Folder and a typed path

Apple's current guide describes the method in one line. In Finder, choose Go > Go to Folder, then start typing a pathname. Matching folders appear as you type. Press Return or double-click the destination, and you are there. The rest of this page fills in the details the one line leaves out, such as how the path characters behave and what to do when nothing matches.
How the path box reads what you type

A path is a list of folder names separated by slashes. Finder reads it from left to right. The first character decides where the path starts. A leading slash (/) starts at the top level of the folder structure. The tilde (~) means your home folder, the one that usually holds Documents, Music and Pictures. Those two starting points cover most of the paths you will type.

A trailing slash is a small detail with a real effect. Apple's guide says a trailing slash marks the entry as a folder. So ~/Documents/ tells Finder you mean the folder itself. Get in the habit of ending a path with a slash when you know the last part is a folder. The list then treats that last part as a folder.

blocks.text: Long paths are easier when you type them in pieces. Type the first folder name, check the list, then add the next name and a slash. The list narrows with every character. You rarely need to recall the full path from memory, which is where typos creep in.
Shortcuts for the folders you open most

Apple's Mac keyboard shortcuts page lists shortcuts for several standard folders. Each one skips the path box entirely. Use them when the folder is one of the standard places. For a folder inside a project, the path box is still faster than clicking through the sidebar.

items: ⌘K opens Connect to Server, for a network share.
⌘↑ opens the folder that contains the current folder.

blocks.text: Apple's shortcuts page shows a published date of September 14, 2026. If a shortcut does nothing on your Mac, check that page against your macOS version before you assume the shortcut is broken. Keep the ones you use most in a note until they feel automatic.
Open Library, the hidden folder

The Library folder is hidden by default, so it does not show up in the normal Finder views. Apple's guide gives a menu route to it. Hold the Option key, click the Go menu, and choose Library. You can also type ~/Library in the Go to Folder box to reach the same place.

blocks.title: Hold Option first
blocks.text: Keep Option held while the Go menu is open. Library shows up in the list only while you hold that key.
Paste a path from another app or a note

Sometimes the path is already in front of you. A colleague sends a path in a chat, or a log file lists where something lives. Copy the path, open the Go to Folder window, press ⌘V, and then press Return. You avoid retyping, and you avoid typos in long folder names with spaces or odd characters.

Check the first character after you paste. A path that starts with ~ or / works as written. If you copied only part of a path, Finder may not find the folder, so compare the text with the path shown in the source. Apple's guide confirms that you can paste a copied pathname and press Return.
Use recent folders instead of retyping

Finder remembers folders you have used. Inside the Go to Folder window, the Up and Down arrows scroll through suggested and recent pathnames. That is faster than typing a folder you visited yesterday. How many recent items the Go menu keeps is a setting. Open Apple menu > System Settings > Menu Bar, and look at Recent documents, applications, and servers. Raise the number there if you want a longer list.
Mistakes people make with Go to Folder

items: Leaving out Shift. The shortcut needs Shift and Command together. Apple lists it as ⇧⌘G.
Typing a name with no starting character. Type ~/Documents, not Documents. Finder reads the first character to decide where to start.
Mixing up / and ~. /Documents starts at the top level of the folder structure. ~/Documents starts in your home folder. They are different places.
Forgetting the trailing slash on a folder. Add a slash after the last name so Finder treats the entry as a folder.
Using Go to Folder to find a file by name. Go to Folder opens folders. To find a file, use Finder search instead.
Assuming the path works on another Mac. A path points to a location on this Mac, so a colleague's Mac may hold a different layout.

blocks.text: When a folder opens with no files or no access

Sometimes the path is correct and the folder still shows nothing useful. Finder may open the folder but show no files, or it may refuse changes inside. The usual cause is permissions. Apple's Get Info window controls who can read and change a folder.

Select the folder, choose File > Get Info, and open the Sharing & Permissions section. Click the lock at the bottom of the panel and authenticate. Pick a user or group, then choose Read & Write, Read only, Write only (Drop Box), or No Access. Read & Write lets you add and change files. Apple's permissions page covers these changes, but it does not explain every error message, so read any dialog closely before you act on it.
Which macOS version this page follows

This page follows Apple's guide, which is labeled macOS 27 Golden Gate. The guide shows no explicit version number or update date, so check your own version. Apple's Mac Help welcome page also covers macOS 27. A 2018 MacMost article describes the same Go to Folder command and the same ⇧⌘G shortcut, so the feature is not new.

blocks.title: Version check
blocks.text: Open the Apple menu and choose About This Mac to see your macOS version before you compare menus with this page.
Where to go next in Finder

Once the folder is open, you may want it closer. The path bar shows where you are at the bottom of the window, which helps when you jump between paths. The sidebar lets you pin a folder you use often. Both have their own steps. See [how to show the path bar in Finder](/how-to/show-the-path-bar-in-finder) and [how to change the sidebar in Finder](/how-to/change-the-sidebar-in-finder).

If the same folder opens every morning, make it the default for new windows. The [default folder guide](/how-to/change-the-default-folder-for-new-windows-in-finder) walks through that setting. If you need a file and cannot recall its folder, use [search for a file in Finder](/how-to/search-for-a-file-in-finder) instead of guessing paths. Hidden files have their own steps in [how to show hidden files in Finder](/how-to/show-hidden-files-in-finder).
Finder is part of macOS, so this method works only on a Mac. Windows uses File Explorer and its own address bar. For a broader look at what Finder does, read the [Finder overview](/apps/finder).

faq.question: Is the shortcut for Go to Folder ⇧⌘G on every Mac?
faq.answer: Apple's keyboard shortcuts page lists Shift Command G as the key for a Go to Folder window. A 2018 MacMost article gives the same keys. Hold both Shift and Command, then press G.

faq.question: Can I use Go to Folder to reach a server or network share?
faq.answer: For a server, use Connect to Server with ⌘K instead. Apple's shortcut list gives ⌘K for it. Go to Folder is meant for folder paths, so open the connect window when you need a network location.

faq.question: What is the difference between ~ and /?
faq.answer: / starts at the top level of the folder structure. ~ starts at your home folder, which usually holds Documents, Music and Pictures. /Documents and ~/Documents are not the same place.

faq.question: Why do I see no suggestions when I type a path?
faq.answer: Check the first character and the spelling. Use ~/ for anything inside your home folder. Remove the last part of the path and type it again slowly to see which level stops matching.

faq.question: Does Go to Folder work on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Finder is the file browser on macOS only. Windows uses File Explorer and its own address bar, so these steps do not apply there.

faq.question: Do these steps work in older macOS versions?
faq.answer: Apple's guide is labeled macOS 27 Golden Gate. A 2018 MacMost article describes the same command and shortcut, so the feature is long established. Check Apple's Mac Help for your version if your menus look different.

faq.question: How do I get back to a folder I used yesterday?
faq.answer: Open the Go to Folder window and use the Up and Down arrows to scroll through recent pathnames. You can also raise the number of recent items under Menu Bar in System Settings.

task: Go to a folder in Finder
appliesTo: Finder on Mac, based on Apple's macOS 27 Golden Gate guide. Other versions not confirmed.
requirements: A Mac with Finder, which is part of macOS
The path to the folder, or the name of a folder you can see in Finder
A keyboard with Shift and Command, or a mouse for the Go menu

steps.name: Make Finder the active app
steps.text: Click the desktop, or click the Finder icon in the Dock. The menu bar should now show Finder at the left, next to the Apple menu. If another app is active, its menus replace Finder's, and the Go menu you need is missing.
steps.tip: Clicking the desktop is the quickest way to make Finder active.

steps.name: Open the Go menu
steps.text: With Finder active, click Go in the menu bar at the top of the screen. The list shows places such as Home, Documents, Downloads and Applications, plus the Go to Folder command.
steps.tip: The Go menu appears only when Finder is the active app.

steps.name: Choose Go to Folder
steps.text: Click Go to Folder. A small window with a text box opens and waits for a path. This is the Go to Folder window, and it accepts typed or pasted text.
steps.tip: Learn the shortcut once, and you can skip the menu on every later visit.

steps.name: Type the start of the path
steps.text: Begin with / to start at the top level of the folder structure, or with ~ to start at your home folder. As you type, matching folders appear in a list under the box. Keep typing names separated by slashes until the folder you want appears in the list.
steps.tip: A trailing slash, as in ~/Documents/, tells Finder the last part is a folder.

steps.name: Accept a suggestion with Tab
steps.text: If a suggestion matches part of the path, press Tab to accept it. Use the Up and Down arrows to scroll through suggested and recent pathnames.
steps.tip: Keep typing when the suggestion is not the folder you want.

steps.name: Open the folder
steps.text: Press Return, or double-click the matching entry in the list. Finder opens that folder in a Finder window, and you can start working with its files.
steps.tip: Double-clicking helps when the list shows several matches and you can see the right name.

steps.name: Paste a path you copied
steps.text: If the path is already on your clipboard, open the Go to Folder window, press ⌘V to paste it, and press Return. Apple's guide confirms that you can paste a copied pathname this way.
steps.tip: Paste works with a path copied from any app that holds text.

troubleshooting.problem: The Go to Folder shortcut does nothing
troubleshooting.fix: Click the desktop first so Finder is the active app, then press ⇧⌘G again. If another app is active, its menus replace Finder's. If the shortcut still fails, use Go > Go to Folder from the menu bar.

troubleshooting.problem: Nothing appears in the list as you type
troubleshooting.fix: Check the first character. Use / for the top level and ~ for your home folder. Type one name at a time, then a slash, to see where the matches stop.

troubleshooting.problem: Finder opens the folder but shows no files
troubleshooting.fix: Check permissions. Select the folder, choose File > Get Info, and open Sharing & Permissions. Click the lock, authenticate, and set your user to Read & Write if you need to change files.

troubleshooting.problem: The folder you need is inside Library
troubleshooting.fix: Hold Option, click Go, and choose Library. You can also type ~/Library in the Go to Folder box.

troubleshooting.problem: The folder is on a server or network share
troubleshooting.fix: Use Go > Connect to Server or press ⌘K. Go to Folder is for folder paths. Check the server address with whoever runs it, because Apple's guides do not cover every network setup.

troubleshooting.problem: Recent folders are missing from the Go menu
troubleshooting.fix: Open Apple menu > System Settings > Menu Bar. Check Recent documents, applications, and servers, and raise the count if you want more recent items.
